item.description: In 1844, official inquiries blamed a price hike to six and a half kreuzer per liter, ignoring the real grievances: apprentices trapped with no advancement, soldiers denied wage bonuses, and the collapse of the guild system.
item.content:encoded:
In 1844, official inquiries blamed a price hike to six and a half kreuzer per liter, ignoring the real grievances: apprentices trapped with no advancement, soldiers denied wage bonuses, and the collapse of the guild system.

Two beer riots—one in Bavaria, one in Chicago—show how beer prices became both flashpoint and scapegoat for deeper social fractures.

3:05 Government-set beer prices guaranteed summer would be more expensive than winter
Bavaria regulated beer brewing under the 1516 Purity Law and set the "Biersatz," an official maximum price per liter, twice yearly. Because summer brewing carried higher costs and steeper taxes, summer prices inevitably exceeded winter prices. This pricing mechanism was supposed to ensure quality and supply, but it had a hidden cost: every rise in the official price was a political decision, directly assignable to the king and cabinet, and directly hittable by public anger.

5:07 In Bavaria, refusing to drink beer meant risking social exclusion
Bavarians treated beer as "liquid bread"—essential caloric intake for the poor. Taverns were where workers networked, found jobs, and built mutual aid. This made cheap beer feel almost like a civic right. Those who refused to drink risked being seen as unsociable or worse, which meant exclusion from both economic and social networks.

9:15 The guild system's collapse left apprentices trapped with nowhere to advance
Munich's population nearly doubled between 1810 and 1840 while Bavaria overall grew about 20%, flooding the city with apprentices and day laborers seeking work. The state took control of guild operations, which stripped guilds of power and resources. The supply of master positions couldn't keep pace with the flood of new apprentices, and most gradually realized they'd never advance to full craftsman status. Trapped in the city without work and unable to afford passage home, many drifted into permanent poverty—a status that was itself a crime, since vagrancy could land them in the poorhouse.

15:26 The beer price hike took effect on the princess's wedding day
In February 1844, the government set summer beer prices at six and a half kreuzer per liter, a full kreuzer jump from the previous year. They announced it in April; it took effect May 1. That day was King Ludwig's daughter Hildegard's wedding. Bavarians already resented the ceremony's modest scale compared to Ludwig's 1810 wedding and felt excluded—poor neighborhoods had been shut out of the festivities. Anonymous placards circulating near the palace included one blunt message: "If you want to afford bread and beer, kill the king." When the price increase went live, it was merely the final straw.

17:27 Soldiers and civilians together destroyed every brewery in Munich
The riot erupted on the wedding night when soldiers at a tavern refused to pay the new price. Thrown out, they signaled with cup-rattling that became a whistle—the command to begin. Rioters smashed windows, overturned tables, shattered chairs. All 33 of Munich's breweries were destroyed, but rioters deliberately left the brewing equipment untouched. The crowds were mostly apprentices and soldiers in similar straits. The soldiers themselves were fresh off losing wage bonuses that had been cancelled during their leave, and many troops ordered to suppress the riot simply refused to fight their peers.

20:33 Official investigators blamed only the price increase, ignoring deeper causes
Engels wrote in the Chartist press, documenting cavalry who refused to mount and police beaten back, and warned that once the public learned violent disorder could reverse government policy, they'd escalate to demands with even higher stakes. Brewers agreed to cut prices on May 2, ending the unrest. But the official inquiry that followed reached a single conclusion: the riot had happened because of the price increase. It said nothing about unemployment, guild decay, or wage theft. Two years later, amid scandal over King Ludwig's relationship with the dancer Lola Montez and the convulsions of 1848 across Europe, Ludwig abdicated.

27:38 Chicago's mayor systematically targeted saloons owned by German and Irish immigrants
Levi Boone, elected mayor in 1855, belonged to the "Know-Nothings," a nativist party hostile to Catholicism and immigration. He enforced the Sunday closing law—but only in immigrant neighborhoods, while the city center operated without interference. He also raised saloon license fees from $50 to $300 and shortened the renewal period from one year to three months. Of Chicago's 675 saloons, 625 were German or Irish-owned. These policies were, in effect, a precision strike on immigrant economic lifelines.

30:46 Immigrant voters united to throw the nativist mayor out of office
In April 1855, a court proceeding became a march on the jail. When authorities opened the Clark Street Bridge against the crowd, both sides opened fire. A police officer lost an arm; the shooter was killed. Sixty people were arrested, fourteen tried, two convicted. License fees fell from $300 to $100. But the political aftershock mattered more: German and Irish immigrants, for the first time, organized as a voting bloc to participate in citywide elections. The next election swept both the Know-Nothing mayor and Know-Nothing aldermen out of office.

item.title: Personal agents won't cannibalize business revenue: lower friction drives more transactions
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-28-ilt-个人智能体不会蚕食企业收入-摩擦越低-交易反而越多/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-28-ilt-个人智能体不会蚕食企业收入-摩擦越低-交易反而越多/
item.description: Instinct's founder says that after reducing checkout friction to nearly zero, transaction frequency between users and merchants rose instead of falling—the opposite of the old ad-driven model.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct's founder says that after reducing checkout friction to nearly zero, transaction frequency between users and merchants rose instead of falling—the opposite of the old ad-driven model.

The founder publicly breaks down trust curves, take-rate models, and scaling strategies for the first time—information-dense.

4:06 No app, only phone and computer
Instinct has no independent application; users interact with it through SMS, voice calls, and email. It has its own phone number and email address, and can even proactively call to send reminders—the founder mentioned that in urgent situations like signing documents, it will proactively tell users it's urgent and there are fewer than ten minutes left. The rationale behind this design choice is: building a new app adds another layer of learning cost for users, while the goal of a personal agent is to replicate ‘social intelligence’—interacting with it like you would with a familiar person, rather than opening yet another tool.

10:22 Agents can also ‘break off’ from each other
Instinct agents can negotiate directly to align schedules, eliminating inefficient back-and-forth between people, but access permissions are tiered: your spouse might have access to almost all information, while colleagues might only see your work calendar. More interestingly, there's an implicit trust mechanism—if the other party overreaches and accesses information they shouldn't, your Instinct will proactively alert you that they've been viewing that category of information, and this relationship's trust level will decrease accordingly. This ‘trusted person network’ is essentially a weighted relationship graph, not simply a friends list.

18:32 Invite-only with small sample volume: $1B+ transactions annually
Instinct remains an invite-only product with a small user base, but the platform's annual transaction volume has exceeded $1 billion, with half coming from travel bookings. The founder gives an example: a user just needs to say ‘I have to be in New York tonight,’ and Instinct automatically identifies their current city, compares airline preferences, seat types, and payment methods, books the flight, then books the hotel, and adds round-trip transportation to the calendar—the user never needs to open any app. He calls this type of end-to-end travel booking a redefinition of the traditional OTA business model.

25:50 After three weeks, 40% of users hand over their credit card
Trust builds not through promises but through time. Data shows that after three weeks of use, 40% of users will proactively provide Instinct with their credit card information; once users have shared at least one sensitive piece of information (credit card, password, etc.), retention jumps to 80%. The founder uses ‘the timing of first sharing sensitive information’ as a proxy metric for trust, and emphasizes that users can always revoke authorized data at any time—this is what he considers the key threshold for whether consumer AI products can be adopted at scale.

32:00 Not a ‘task executor’: rejecting the ad model
Noah explicitly states he doesn't want Instinct to follow the old ‘free plus ads’ path—if an agent smarter than users and more savvy socially convinces them to buy things they don't actually want, that's a dangerous reality. So Instinct isn't simply a tool for executing commands, but is trained to pursue higher-level objectives—building trust for users, making them feel cared for, even if that means giving up some short-term revenue from persuading them to purchase more. This is also why the business model ultimately landed on transaction-based take rates rather than ads or subscription.

42:32 Friction drops to zero, transactions actually increase
Intuitively, an agent taking over ordering should damage the interests of companies like Uber Eats and DoorDash that monetize user attention. But Noah points out the counterexample: throughout history, every reduction in checkout clicks has been followed by rising transaction volume, and Instinct can reduce friction to nearly zero—for instance, if your calendar shows you'll be late, the car will auto-arrange early; if you get home without eating, it proactively asks if you want that dish you ordered last time. He calls this a counterintuitive game: users spend less time in apps, but actual transaction frequency with merchants actually increases.

58:54 Compute must be provisioned months ahead; betting wrong costs three to four times more
Instinct's daily active demand itself doubles every week, and compute delivery cycles are measured in months—unlike other consumer products where you can scale resources in line with user growth. Noah describes the difficulty of this decision: buying 2x capacity gets consumed immediately, buying 5x runs out in three weeks, buying 10x carries high-leverage risk—if you judge wrong, excess compute gets forfeited at three to four times the price. He says 40% of his time is spent agonizing over exactly how far ahead to buy and how much to procure.

1:03:59 Proactive agents need an order of magnitude more compute than code-writing products
Unlike programming agents like Cursor or Codex, where users ask questions, the model does work, and then returns results, Instinct's architecture allows it to wake up at any point during the day and decide on its own whether to bother the user—for example, scanning the day's schedule at dawn, finding something worth reminding about in the afternoon, then proactively reaching out to the user. Noah believes this native proactivity means the required compute is an order of magnitude higher than initially thought, and the industry's current compute buildout has barely scratched the surface of what proactive work demands.

item.title: AI Coding Tools Code Faster, But Software Itself Hasn't Gotten Smarter in a Decade
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-28-a16z-ai编码工具写代码更快-但软件本身十年没怎么变聪明/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-28-a16z-ai编码工具写代码更快-但软件本身十年没怎么变聪明/
item.description: Coding agents let people code faster, but they produce the same kind of software. Diogo Almeida argues what we should really do is make AI a new primitive in software, automating things that previously couldn't be automated.
item.content:encoded:
Coding agents let people code faster, but they produce the same kind of software. Diogo Almeida argues what we should really do is make AI a new primitive in software, automating things that previously couldn't be automated.

A founder shares his journey from early-stage AGI disillusionment at OpenAI to building Jev, clarifying the fundamental difference between AI-native programming and traditional coding agents.

3:02 Coding agents and Jev solve fundamentally different problems
Cloud Code and Codex represent "just in time software"—writing code in natural language produces output equivalent to code written by humans, with unchanged expressiveness. Diogo's vision isn't faster coding but a new AI primitive embedded in software itself: not automating "software engineering" as a job, but automating tasks that should be automated but currently aren't. That changes what software itself can do.

7:11 Jev is a classifier, but that's not a limitation
Diogo explicitly describes Jev as a classifier—this is precise technical language, not dismissive. It's more akin to a library: you describe desired behavior in natural language, pair it with a state machine, and Jev selects branches with confidence scores. He estimates current Jev likely already outperforms what a traditional ML engineering team in 2019 would ship after months of dataset collection and model tuning—and ordinary developers can now "write" this capability on the spot.

12:19 We're building products, not creating deity
Ben Horowitz cited TypeSafe's phrase "we build prod, not God" as its most compelling insight. Other large-model labs, even privately, revel in the weighty narrative that "we are creating potentially uncontrollable technology." TypeSafe inverts this—AI optimism is simply put on the table. Diogo traces much of the industry's pessimism to the "single brain rules everything" myth: if you believe only one ever-larger centralized model represents AI's future, it's hard to grasp why developers get excited about a programmable AI primitive.

18:25 He believed GPT was AGI until his entire worldview collapsed
Diogo participated in releasing early RLHF models at OpenAI and hadn't anticipated instruction-tuning's generalization strength. The team deliberately tested with ‘why should you eat socks before meditating’—a question guaranteed never to appear on the internet—and the model produced sensible, human-like answers. He genuinely believed this model probably was AGI. When it wasn't, he describes it as a moment his ‘entire worldview collapsed,’ and the inflection point toward his later conviction that AI should be genuinely useful, not merely appear intelligent.

19:26 Disbelieves recursive self-improvement but sees AGI through a different lens
Diogo explicitly states that for various complex reasons, he doesn't believe AI follows a recursive self-improvement path—neither in the past nor now. However, he does endorse OpenAI's simpler definition of AGI: automating most economically valuable work globally. This is entirely feasible since much valuable economic work is actually basic and repetitive. The real problem emerged post-RLHF: industry focused energy on satisfying a "human rater" proxy metric. GPT-3 was initially well-calibrated, but with humans scoring outputs, the model increasingly produced eloquent text without proportionally improving at actual task automation.

24:39 Customer service stalls at the long tail, not at intelligence limits
Diogo points to OpenAI's customer service automation efforts since 2020 as a counterexample: intelligence already suffices—so why hasn't it worked? Martin offers a precise observation from early customer service company data: they'd claim ‘we resolve 95% of tickets,’ which sounds impressive until you deduplicate by content and find only ~50% are unique problems; the rest are password resets and other high-frequency repeats. The bottleneck isn't model smartness. The real world naturally follows long-tail distribution—standard chatbots can handle the head, not the exceptions in the tail.

26:42 Reliable systems don't need to produce identical outputs every time
Diogo breaks reliability into three layers. Layer one approximates traditional availability and SLA metrics. Layer two approaches "determinism," but he stresses this matters for unit tests, not real systems—for instance, include a UUID in a prompt and outputs are functionally equivalent but literally different. For the third layer he hasn't yet settled on terminology; call it "robustness"—not requiring identical answers, but requiring each answer to be a judgment that would make sense to a human. He contends that each additional "9" in reliability unlocks an entirely new category of applications previously too risky for AI deployment.

33:49 The SaaS doomsday thesis overlooked a key detail: major PRs are tiny
When coding agents arrived, markets feared SaaS displacement and stock prices fell accordingly. Jev's emergence prompted collective SaaS celebration—because while "software is cheap" is true, "therefore easily replaced" is wrong. Enormous value lies in invisible engineering details. Ben Horowitz adds a calibrating observation: a typical major pull request at a large company contains ~10 lines of actual code. Coding agents automate writing those 10 lines, not adding new capability. Jev provides a new primitive that lets software grow functionality that didn't previously exist. This explains why AI-written code is faster but software itself hasn't improved—and why less review now means more security risk.

item.content:encoded:
Five years ago customer acquisition cost was one-tenth of today; Aodo's one-year payback on pillows rode that wave—now Huazhu, despite greater scale, can't match that launch speed.

For anyone judging whether consumer tracks still have opportunity windows; the industry background is lengthy, but you can jump straight to the Aodo and Superbowl sections.

2:01 K-Pro aims to hit 1,000 stores—a strategic commitment, not a test
The K-Pro name was registered pre-pandemic but remained uncommitted until 2024, when it locked in as a light-meal brand. By end of 2025 it had fewer than 200 locations; this year it's targeted 500, and by next H1 over 1,000. More revealing: across KFC's entire system over many years, the group has hand-built only two new brands itself—K-Coffee and K-Pro—signaling that light meals rank as a strategic tier second only to coffee, not just a test.

6:02 Shoulder-to-shoulder expansion saves two layers of cost
K-Pro and K-Coffee don't scout locations independently. They open extra kitchens and counter zones inside KFC's already-negotiated locations, serving different customer needs at the same point. Two benefits: first, they inherit KFC's mass-market brand gravity, so the new brand doesn't build awareness from zero; second, they compress costs—the same staff, POS system, cleaning protocols, and logistics all spread thin, and rent for the expanded footprint doesn't double.

14:08 Light meals took time because fresh vegetables are a logistics nightmare
Beef-noodle chains and Mixue (米雪冰城) scaled to ten-thousand-store chains on pre-packaged components; expansion was ferocious. But light meals depend intrinsically on fresh vegetables—the hardest category to manage, most prone to spoilage, nearly impossible to standardize through central kitchens. Brands usually avoid it entirely until health demand spiked enough to make unit economics work. That's when KFC finally entered the game—and it's become nearly a weather vane for the whole sector.

18:10 KFC is a laggard in America, a powerhouse in China
KFC and Pizza Hut are both waning in the U.S. KFC doesn't crack the top three quick-service chains; Pizza Hut is worse. Recently Yum's U.S. HQ sold Pizza Hut outright for $2.7 billion. In China, KFC outnumbers McDonald's by over 50%. The divergence: Yum China was spun off early to operate independently and listed separately in Hong Kong, with HQ not remote-controlling strategy. That autonomy is why homegrown innovations like K-Coffee and K-Pro can keep launching.

24:11 Superbowl wins on cheap, not nostalgia
Superbowl's ticket was 30+ yuan—not objectively cheap. But early investor research found core users saw it as a money-saver: for the same healthy meal, they'd previously paid 60-70 or 70-80 yuan at Wagas-type concepts. Once a consumer commits to eating healthy, they don't compare to a 20-yuan beef noodle; they shop within healthy options for the cheapest alternative. That gap gave a seemingly pricey light-meal brand room to grow.

43:25 One pillow sold ¥3 billion last year
Aodo Star (亚朵星球) posted ¥3.6 billion in sleep product revenue in 2025; the pillow alone—one signature SKU—drove over ¥3 billion. At an average price around ¥300, that's nearly 10 million units sold. This year, facing headwinds from subsidy phase-out and KOL-driven gifting pullback, Aodo still projects 25-30% growth, pushing revenue close to ¥5 billion. Scale this large strains calling it a ‘second curve’—it's now a core business line rivaling the hotel.

52:34 Mattress covers replace fitted sheets; small innovation still pays
Home textiles lived off real estate and urbanization windfalls for years—no product innovation needed, so design talent was scarce. Aodo had to recruit from apparel, where fabric work moves faster. The changes looked tiny: a fitted mattress cover that snaps on in ten seconds, replacing fussy tucked sheets; duvets without tie knots. Industry had ignored these details until now. They've become consensus.

1:03:40 Aodo's payback speed is unreplicable today
Aodo took just over a year from pillow launch to break-even—already remarkably fast for a consumer product. But from 2022 to 2026, customer acquisition cost has risen 10x or more, while product price can't follow suit. Today, even Huazhu (华住) with 2x Aodo's unit count and major capital deployed to the same play would struggle to break even in a year-plus; more likely three years minimum. Most founders don't have that patience.

item.description: A developer wins crosswalk approval, only to be told construction will take years—or much longer—with quotes running into the millions. It precisely exposes what's really true: LA's approval system looks permissive but is actually gridlocked everywhere.
item.content:encoded:
A developer wins crosswalk approval, only to be told construction will take years—or much longer—with quotes running into the millions. It precisely exposes what's really true: LA's approval system looks permissive but is actually gridlocked everywhere.

A live conversation about LA neighborhoods, zoning, and the crosswalk approval farce. The information density isn't high, but the Kafkaesque details and concrete specifics—parking, transformer shortages—are worth hearing.

1:04 Developers Want New Buildings to Be Anticipated, Not Feared
Zach Lazzari came from theater and performance; when he moved to LA in 2014, he noticed that whenever new construction scaffolding went up on a block, residents' instinct was usually: "Oh no, what are they building now?" He thinks this shouldn't be the baseline. Commercial real estate should curate tenants the way A24 scouts directors—finding people with a vision—not replicate another Shake Shack. He has nothing against Shake Shack; there just doesn't need to be one everywhere.

3:06 Low Density Is Why LA's Shops Are Independent
Bill McBride argues that high density in New York forces high rents for the same location, but LA's sprawl spreads things out, which is exactly why mom-and-pop shops survive there—his own neighborhood along the Pacific Coast Highway is almost entirely independent. Zach adds that many talented friends who went to school in New York later moved to LA because home-buying costs too much there, but LA makes it easier to find solid rent in an interesting neighborhood, letting people focus on their work instead of being crushed by housing.

7:08 Zoning Is the Developer's Real Biggest Problem
Bill says if you ask home builders or apartment developers, zoning is always the biggest puzzle piece. California's new ADU rules have bumped housing supply slightly, but truly changing zoning is hard. He gives an example: after California declared an official housing crisis, new rules banned density reduction—previously someone could buy three consecutive houses in a coastal community, tear them down, and build a real mansion, causing density to drop. That path is now closed.

9:09 Buy the Whole Block; Build the Neighborhood Like Jacobs Wrote It
Zach says the Western and Melrose project drew inspiration mainly from Jane Jacobs' "The Death and Life of Great American Cities," which describes Greenwich Village streets as a "sidewalk ballet." He grew up seeing this kind of neighborhood in New York, where you could walk and feel culture; LA almost never has a main street like that, and on the rare occasion it does, it ends up like an airport mall. The constraint is that ~95% of LA's urban land is zoned residential, so once the culture and life drain from the main street, the surrounding area is just pure housing—nowhere to go.

11:11 Rates Shifted; Commercial Real Estate Can't Profit on Spread Anymore
Zach believes commercial real estate used to run on "financial engineering"—assemble a room of 140-IQ people with spreadsheets, pocket the spread between capitalization rate and interest rate, and turn a profit. But now rates are higher than the cap rate when the building was bought, so that math doesn't work, forcing developers to actually make a good product. His project's rents are rising precisely because he invested in design talent, rather than the way most new apartments do—turning out bland, forgettable buildings.

13:21 Getting a Crosswalk Built Is Like a Kafka Novel
Zach complains that applying to build a crosswalk in LA is "like a Kafka novel." They got approval for the Clinton and Western intersection, but the email said completion would be "years from now or longer." When they pushed back, there was no actual process—the city said yes, but engineering, electrical, plus burying an underground conduit box below ran into millions of dollars in quotes, as if asking, "What else can you do for us?"

16:23 ADUs Don't Need Parking, Yet Streets Get More Crowded
Bill notes that California's new ADU rules have a side effect: these backyard units don't require off-site parking spaces, so neighborhoods that build ADUs end up with streets fuller of cars than before. Zach adds that he hasn't driven in years and used to underestimate how much parking matters to LA people—friends would rather move their car half a block away to avoid a hard-to-park shopping area, and places like Fairfax, where parking is so bad that people simply give up shopping, aren't rare.

17:26 Koreatown's Parking Might Be the World's Most Insane
Bill says parking in Koreatown might be one of the most insane scenes on Earth—constantly zero open spots. His wife lived there and saw people just sit in their car next to a space, then immediately coordinate to swoop in if someone leaves. They note that self-driving cars would dramatically ease parking once widespread, ugly garage entrances could disappear, and even speeding-ticket revenue would take a hit.
